This debugging session is primarily divided into two parts:

Part One introduces the basic debugging process and related standards, including the definition of debugging, its scope of application, applicable codes and standards, as well as the responsibilities of debugging institutions or agents.

Part Two covers the schedule for debugging, cost structure, and training arrangements after project completion.

Commissioning refers to the process of verifying, testing, and validating mechanical systems, electrical systems, etc., after the substantial completion of a project. Commissioning must be executed in accordance with the project design or the owner’s requirements, involving not only the operational validation of the entire system post-construction but also extensive documentation. These documents record the entire commissioning process, including issues identified and resolved, and are ultimately delivered to the owner as part of the project handover files for future operation and maintenance reference.

The difference between Testing and Commissioning lies in: Testing typically focuses on functional checks of individual systems, equipment, or components; whereas Commissioning is a comprehensive validation of the entire project system, accompanied by extensive documentation. Additionally, Commissioning begins during the design phase, requiring review of the designer’s deliverables and providing feedback, as well as participation in project scheduling; Testing, however, is conducted only after equipment installation for physical validation.

This article primarily discusses Building Commissioning. Building Commissioning mainly involves critical systems such as electrical and mechanical systems. Other fields, such as industrial projects, have their own commissioning processes.

The system also includes the airtightness and waterproof performance of the building envelope, as well as life safety systems. Depending on the purpose of building commissioning, it can be further subdivided.

The system also includes the airtightness and waterproof performance of the building envelope, as well as life safety systems. Depending on the purpose of building commissioning, it can be further subdivided.

Safety, energy efficiency, and environmental sustainability are all critical factors that need to be considered. Quantity surveying offers numerous advantages, such as reducing the likelihood and number of change orders or conflicts during construction. As commissioning agents or authoritative bodies, they conduct reviews as early as the detailed design phase (i.e., the 66% design stage). These reviews focus not only on technical aspects but also emphasize the constructability of the design—the feasibility of implementing the design on-site.

Is the design energy-efficient? Does it avoid energy waste? During the commissioning process, are factors for future maintenance and operation considered? This is highly beneficial to the design itself. Additionally, commissioning ensures that systems and equipment are installed strictly according to design requirements and owner needs, while verifying whether commissioning, operation, and maintenance meet the owner’s or project’s design specifications. The commissioning process involves comprehensive validation of every piece of equipment, system, and component, achieving 100% coverage, which is critical for the final handover of the project.

Commissioning is also a quality management tool. The involvement of commissioning agents and authoritative bodies enhances project management and coordination efficiency. Issues identified from a commissioning perspective provide design consultants with review feedback and offer valuable recommendations to the project management team, making project execution more thorough, comprehensive, and efficient while avoiding oversights or delays.

Commissioning can also uncover issues with installed equipment and systems, enabling timely repairs—especially for building automation or mechanical systems related to energy efficiency. By adjusting building automation programming or operational methods, building energy performance can be optimized. The extensive documentation generated during commissioning records all systems, equipment, and test results, serving as a crucial reference for future operation, maintenance, and equipment replacement.

Commissioning is not limited to new construction.

Commissioning is not limited to new construction. Some projects also involve the commissioning of existing buildings. This commissioning aims to identify issues in the building’s mechanical, electrical, and other systems, including the building envelope, whether they are hardware problems with the equipment systems themselves or software-related issues in operational methods, such as software in the BIS system.

During summer cooling, if the outdoor air is relatively cool, the supply air temperature of the air conditioning unit is reset based on the outdoor ambient temperature to avoid energy waste and achieve energy savings. Another example is the nighttime and daytime operating modes of a building automation system, corresponding to occupied and unoccupied states. When offices are unoccupied, excessive comfort levels are not required. In summer, indoor temperatures can be set to 26–28°C, and fewer air conditioning units operate at night. During the day, temperatures are maintained at around 22°C, with similar adjustments in winter. This approach significantly reduces energy consumption.

Conducting such commissioning for existing buildings enhances building performance while lowering energy costs. Energy-saving measures reduce the consumption of electricity, natural gas, and other energy sources, as well as daily maintenance expenses. Additionally, operational costs decrease, which includes not only energy expenses but also personnel costs for operations and maintenance. Before achieving building automation, a large number of maintenance staff might have been required. After automation, the demand for personnel is greatly reduced—the higher the automation level, the fewer the personnel needed, thereby cutting labor costs.

Enhancing user comfort is one of the key objectives. Additionally, there is a method called “Retrospective Re-Commissioning”, which essentially involves conducting a comprehensive audit and recommissioning of existing systems.

This differs from the previously mentioned commissioning. For existing buildings, commissioning must be based on the current equipment conditions. During recommissioning, a thorough audit of existing equipment is required, including understanding the current configuration and operational status.

In contrast, commissioning for New Construction is different because relevant information is already available during the design phase. The commissioning agent participates from the installation stage and is highly familiar with the entire system. Commissioning existing buildings presents more challenges: the commissioning team may be unfamiliar with both hardware and software, and building documentation is often incomplete. To understand system or equipment performance, technical documents such as construction drawings or operation manuals must be consulted, but these materials may be difficult to obtain for existing buildings, requiring significant time to gather information.

In comparison, new construction projects have complete documentation from the outset, including all manufacturer information. Project types requiring commissioning include New Construction, among others.

New construction projects require commissioning, including complex buildings as well as existing ones. However, the private sector does not necessarily conduct commissioning due to the additional costs involved. In contrast, the public sector or government agencies, such as hospitals, schools, and government office buildings, typically commission existing structures to enhance comfort and energy efficiency.

Commissioning work primarily involves mechanical and electrical systems and equipment. It can be categorized into several major types, including vertical transportation such as elevators, and building envelope commissioning. Building envelope commissioning focuses on identifying air or water leaks in walls, with the primary goal of enhancing energy efficiency. Energy savings are achieved not only through mechanical and electrical systems but also significantly depend on the building envelope. Factors such as insulation type, number of window glazing layers, and door specifications have a substantial impact on energy usage efficiency.

In previous years, LEED certification was quite popular in North America, involving many LEED-specific commissioning processes. This type of commissioning did not focus particularly on mechanical or electrical systems but rather on compliance with standards—such as the proportion of locally sourced materials, the use of renewable energy, and adherence to LEED clauses. This differed from conventional commissioning. However, LEED commissioning has declined in North America in recent years because LEED certification peaked in popularity from two decades ago to ten years ago. Nowadays, the emphasis has shifted toward substantive energy-saving measures in construction rather than some of the less practical aspects of LEED.

The above provides an overview of which projects require commissioning. It is also essential to follow relevant codes and standards during the process.

In Canada, there is the CSA Z320 Standard, which pertains to building commissioning standards and checklists. ASHRAE also has numerous standards or guidelines related to commissioning, including the commissioning process and HVAC commissioning procedures.

First, there is the general process, followed by specific procedures for HVAC systems. Additionally, there is an organization abroad called the Building Commissioning Association, which functions like an industry association, providing resources such as commissioning manuals, samples, and templates.

In the United States, the commissioning standard for electrical equipment is ANSI/NETA ATS, which stands for Standard for Acceptance Testing Specifications for Electrical Power Equipment and Systems.

In Canada, the S1001 Standard (Integrated Systems Testing of Fire Protection and Life Safety Systems) became mandatory approximately three to four years ago as a specialized commissioning and testing standard for fire protection systems. This standard has now been incorporated into building codes, making such commissioning and testing a requirement for nearly all buildings.

The system includes fire pumps, jockey pumps, and pressure systems such as smoke exhaust fans and positive pressure air supply systems. Additionally, it incorporates equipment like fire elevators, forming a complete integrated system. During a fire incident, the operation of mechanical systems, electrical systems, and elevator systems must be comprehensively evaluated. Our company has extensive experience in commissioning such systems, particularly excelling in settings like garment factories.

There are few professionals engaged in this type of commissioning, primarily for two reasons:  
1. Fire protection systems are strictly regulated in both North America and China, requiring significant responsibility and risk-taking post-commissioning.  
2. The system involves multi-disciplinary coordination, making it highly complex. Many mechanical professionals lack knowledge of electrical systems, and vice versa, resulting in a scarcity of cross-disciplinary commissioning talent. Some individuals avoid taking responsibility due to a lack of confidence, fearing operational errors.

In Canada, commissioning for fire protection systems has been a mandatory requirement for the past three years. The two documents—the PSPC Commissioning Manual and PSPC Commissioning Guidelines—were developed by the Canadian federal government specifically for commissioning its government projects. The industry commonly refers to the roles of “Commissioning Authority” or “Commissioning Agent,” which originate from these standards.

Whether an individual or a company, as the commissioning leader, one must organize commissioning activities and oversee the entire commissioning process while assuming full responsibility. They need to organize, lead, and oversee the entire debugging process.

He needs to organize, lead, and oversee the entire debugging process.

During the commissioning process, it is necessary to review all testing and commissioning activities and prepare relevant reports. Simultaneously, coordination with various professional stakeholders is required, including the Client, consultants, general contractors, subcontractors, as well as startup personnel and technicians from equipment manufacturers.

The Commissioning Agent (CxA) does not directly participate in commissioning operations but is responsible for supervision and coordination to ensure all processes comply with requirements. Ultimately, all commissioning documents must be consolidated into a handover package and submitted to the Client.

Internationally, especially for large or complex projects, commissioning agencies are typically hired directly by the Client, operating independently of consultants and contractors, and are referred to as Third-Party Commissioning Agents (3rd Party CxA). Their responsibilities include reviewing design drawings to ensure construction and commissioning quality meet the Client’s requirements and design specifications. This mechanism effectively prevents contractors from misreporting progress and ensures every system and equipment functions properly.

Currently, such third-party commissioning agencies are relatively common in Canada and the U.S. but have yet to form a mature system in China. This model has been applied internationally for approximately two to three decades, providing professional assurance to Clients through independent Commissioning Authorities (CxAs) or agents.

Sometimes, appointing an agent also requires certain designated procedures.

Sometimes, appointing an agent also requires certain designated procedures.

In the engineering field, professional certification is not mandatory. For example, the Building Commissioning Certified Professional (BCxP) is similar to PMP but not required. Additionally, the CPP certification falls into the same category. In actual projects, although we have encountered numerous cases, situations requiring these certifications are extremely rare.

Project scale and complexity determine whether a third-party Commissioning Agent (Cx Agent) needs to be engaged. For large and complex projects, an independent third-party Cx Agent is typically required, rather than relying on contractors or consulting firms. For small to medium-sized projects, cost control may lead to consulting firms with professional capabilities taking on the dual role of Cx Agent. If the consulting firm lacks the necessary expertise, the client will need to separately appoint a third party.

Regarding the timing of commissioning activities, planning should be based on the specific characteristics of the project. Large and complex projects must involve a third-party Commissioning Authority throughout the entire process, with their involvement timing determined in accordance with standards such as ASHRAE.

Typically, the Commissioning Agent gets involved when 66% of the Design Development drawings are completed during the design phase. At this stage, the Commissioning Agent needs to review the 66% drawings and provide comments, while also participating in design review meetings. During the design phase, the Commissioning Agent is not only responsible for reviews but also for preparing commissioning deliverables, including documents such as the Commissioning Plan, Commissioning Specification, and Commissioning Form. Later, examples of these standard documents will be shown.

During the design phase, it is necessary to define the scope of future commissioning systems, commissioning methods, team composition, and commissioning plans, including training arrangements. Additionally, commissioning requirements must be established, and the Commissioning Specification for the contract must be generated. Commissioning meetings and testing procedures also need to be planned in advance, specifying test steps for different equipment and systems, as well as detailed requirements for test documentation, including forms and format standards.

These tasks are typically completed by the 99% design stage, i.e., before the release of tender documents and construction documents. These contents will be included as part of the tender package, and the contractor will clarify the scope of commissioning work upon securing the contract. The actual commissioning work is carried out by the contractor or testing contractor under the guidance of the Commissioning Agent.

Regarding the system and equipment commissioning work, the specific operations are handled by the testing contractor, not the commissioning agent. The primary responsibilities of the commissioning agent are supervision, management, and guidance, ultimately reviewing results, consolidating information, and generating reports. Additionally, they are responsible for coordinating project schedules and scope.

Commissioning work must be arranged based on on-site conditions and project progress. The mobilization time depends on the overall project advancement and on-site installation status. Typically, commissioning begins when the project reaches the substantial completion stage—meaning the main construction is finished and major equipment installation is complete, with only minor finishing work remaining. In practice, the commissioning agent must conduct on-site inspections before substantial completion to assess installation quality and progress issues.

The core work of the commissioning agent is concentrated in the later commissioning phase, when the project is nearing completion. At this stage, comprehensive commissioning of all systems and equipment is required, and the duration is affected by uncontrollable factors. If equipment malfunctions or system anomalies are discovered, they must be reported to the client and the design consultant for modifications, which may extend the commissioning period. Ideally, only minor issues need addressing, making the commissioning process smoother.

When encountering major equipment or system problems, the commissioning agent must collaborate with the client and the design consultant to resolve them, which may involve equipment replacement or system modifications. Once all systems are verified, reports are submitted, and training is completed, the end user can move in. The exact timing depends on the complexity of the systems.

The scale of the project and whether any major issues arise will both impact the progress. In previous sessions, the engineer inquired about the time required for the project, and a timeline was provided. In reality, this demands significant effort and time, especially for large-scale projects.

If it is required that every system and piece of equipment be fully commissioned and undergo comprehensive functional testing, a substantial amount of work must be completed. The specific commissioning process needs to be coordinated with other project stakeholders. For example, before commissioning the air handling units, it is necessary to confirm whether the PM has completed the installation, including the provision of water, electricity, and gas. Additionally, it is essential to consult with the client and advisory units to determine their involvement in the commissioning process.

Typically, a notice period of 7 to 10 days is required, while government departments demand an even longer lead time. During commissioning, it is crucial to confirm the presence of relevant contractors, such as control system contractors and equipment manufacturers, and to prepare the necessary tools and equipment. At the same time, the commissioning schedule must be communicated with the on-site construction team to assess potential impacts. The approximate cost range for commissioning services should also be considered.

The determination of commissioning fees depends on the project’s complexity, client type, and the country or region. Typically, commissioning service fees account for 3% to 8% of the cost of the equipment and systems being commissioned. For example, in a project with a total cost of 1 million yuan, if the MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing) systems cost 300,000 yuan and only the MEP systems require commissioning, the commissioning fee would be approximately 24,000 yuan (calculated at 8%).

It is important to note that commissioning work not only involves on-site inspections of equipment and system operations but also includes extensive documentation, coordination, design reviews, and final document integration, requiring significant time and effort. Additionally, relevant training must be provided to the client as the commissioning process nears completion.

Finally, the training for the Owner’s Operations and Maintenance (O&M) team is a critical phase. Typically arranged as commissioning nears completion, the training is usually conducted by the Contractor, such as Rockwell Automation’s Control Contractor, or technical personnel from equipment suppliers like Honeywell, as they possess the deepest system familiarity.

Participants primarily include the Owner’s O&M team, and sometimes Owner representatives and end-user delegates. For instance, in an office building project, each tenant unit must send representatives to attend training covering topics like HVAC system operation, building system overviews, and fire alarm procedures. For a Two-Stage Fire Alarm system, users must be trained to distinguish between pre-alarm and actual fire alarm sound patterns.

Training for the O&M team delves deeper, covering Rockwell graphical interface navigation, setpoint adjustments, screen editing, and programming. For fire protection systems, additional training includes handling false alarms, muting alarms, and reset procedures.

The training is typically organized by the Owner’s PM, Cx Agent, or Construction Manager. Large-scale projects may have a dedicated Commissioning Manager to coordinate. Sessions generally last at least 2 hours, while complex systems may require days or even 1–2 weeks. For example, a Tianjin project involved a week-long training program.

A comprehensive Training Log must document details like training content, dates, attendee lists, and signed acknowledgments.

This concludes the first part of the commissioning explanation. Please raise any questions if you have them.

Who should be responsible for the training work?

The system commissioning work is primarily the responsibility of the equipment manufacturers or contractors, as they are more familiar with the system. Regarding the operation and performance of each specific system and equipment, manufacturers or contractors have a better understanding than the owner.

For example, in building automation projects, the control contractor is typically responsible for programming and testing. If a local company acts as a Honeywell product agent and undertakes the project, it may have its own technical team to complete these tasks. The training portion is handled by the control contractor or the local company, while large-scale projects may receive direct training services from Honeywell.

The general contractor is accountable to the owner and must provide training for the owner’s operations and maintenance team. If the general contractor lacks the capability to conduct training, they may coordinate with Honeywell or its local agents to organize a training team. The training includes test support during the commissioning phase, and relevant contractors must be on-site to complete all tasks under the guidance of the commissioning agent or the competent authority. Therefore, the training is primarily carried out by the equipment manufacturers.

The training cost is already included in the product price, so no additional training fees are required.

The training cost is already included in the product price, so no additional training fees are required.

During the design phase, the client typically hires consultants to prepare the design, which ultimately forms the tender documents. The tender documents will explicitly state that the contractor must include training costs and commissioning/testing fees in their quotation. If the contractor overlooks these requirements, mistakenly assuming that commissioning and training costs are not included, they cannot evade responsibility when the client later requests these services.

As the Main Contractor, when collaborating with Subcontractors (such as Hone Yard), it is essential to clearly define the allocation of commissioning, testing, and training costs in the subcontract agreement while signing the main contract with the client. These costs are usually substantial, and if not explicitly stipulated in the contract, the subcontractor will assume they are excluded, leaving the main contractor to bear unexpected additional expenses.

Therefore, it is crucial to clearly delineate the responsibility for commissioning, testing, and training costs in the contract.

Now we officially begin the second part, which will provide a detailed explanation of the specific content.

First, we will discuss the systems and equipment that require commissioning. Next, the responsibilities and obligations of each participating party (Each Party) during the commissioning process, namely their Scope of Work. Additionally, the documents to be submitted upon completion of commissioning, as well as the Commissioning Agent’s scope of work.

The required Inputs for providing commissioning Deliverables, along with the test results and reports (Testing Results/Reports) that the commissioning agent needs to obtain from the Contractors. This commissioning primarily involves mechanical systems and equipment (System/Equipment).

The system primarily consists of three major components:

Air System (iTrack): Includes equipment such as air handling units (AHUs) and VAV boxes.

The system primarily consists of three major components:

Air System (iTrack): Includes equipment such as air handling units (AHUs) and VAV boxes.

Water System: Divided into plumbing systems and fire protection systems. The fire protection system comprises sprinkler systems and standpipe systems, equipped with fire pumps and pressure maintenance pumps. Additionally, the central plant houses boilers, chiller systems, circulation pumps, and cooling towers.

Electrical System: Covers lighting, power supply, fire alarm systems (including emergency power), and low-voltage systems (e.g., communication, security). The Building Automation System (BAS) requires separate handling due to its cross-disciplinary complexity in MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) and vendor-specific variations (programming platforms, communication protocols, hardware).

Elevator commissioning is a key focus. While not entirely classified under life safety, it adheres to stringent safety standards, with firefighter elevators subject to even higher requirements.

Life Safety may operate independently or be integrated within MEP/elevator systems, encompassing the aforementioned related components.

Building Envelope involves the design of exterior walls, basement waterproofing, and roof waterproofing, including material selection (e.g., wall thickness, window types) and energy efficiency compliance (e.g., international standards like Energy Specialist).

The software calculates energy demand through computer modeling. Energy specialists need to coordinate with multiple parties: first, discussing building structures and layouts with architects; second, finalizing mechanical system plans with mechanical engineers; and lastly, communicating with building environment experts. Based on the mathematical model results from energy specialists, they evaluate whether the expected energy-saving effects can be achieved. Local building codes have clearly defined energy efficiency standards, and only projects meeting these requirements can obtain construction permits.

Taking Vancouver as an example, the city implements a “Net Zero Energy” policy. If a building achieves energy self-sufficiency, the government grants additional floor area incentives. For instance, a 4,000-square-foot lot could be expanded to 6,000 square feet upon meeting net-zero standards. Several of our projects have accomplished this by installing solar panels on rooftops. When solar power generation meets the entire building’s electricity demand, it qualifies as net-zero compliant.

For developers, adding 2,000 square feet of floor area translates to approximately CAD 2 million in additional revenue, while solar panel installation costs only CAD 200,000–500,000, offering significant economic benefits. Additionally, commissioning must account for life safety codes and building envelope requirements.

Debugging work must be conducted according to seasonal characteristics. For example, HVAC system commissioning requires distinguishing between winter and summer conditions: winter focuses on heating system testing, while summer emphasizes refrigeration system testing. During winter commissioning, refrigeration equipment such as chillers cannot be tested, so additional time must be scheduled to complete testing for these devices.

Equipment startup refers to the commissioning procedures for complex equipment such as air handling units, chillers, boilers, generators, or high/low-voltage switchgear. Before formal commissioning, the factory test reports provided by manufacturers must be reviewed to confirm the equipment’s normal factory condition, which is also a critical part of the commissioning process.

An HVAC system consists of multiple subsystems: the ventilation system requires air balancing (HVAC air balancing) commissioning; the central plant includes core equipment such as boilers and chillers. The plumbing system covers various pumps and rotary pumps. The fire protection system falls under life safety and includes standard fire exits and sprinkler systems. Additionally, the pressurization system and smoke exhaust system (ventilation system) also fall within the scope of mechanical equipment commissioning.

All the above systems must be commissioned in compliance with regulatory requirements.

The electrical system is already familiar to everyone and will not be elaborated on here. The fire alarm system, emergency power supply, low-voltage system, etc., will also not be explained in detail.

However, the AHJ inspection report from the competent authority is mandatory. This report only verifies whether the installation complies with electrical design codes and building codes, and does not cover the commissioning and testing phases.

Energy-saving commissioning involves complex systems and equipment. The commissioning work primarily focuses on mechanical and electrical systems as well as fire protection systems, such as LEED certification and energy efficiency requirements. What are the roles and responsibilities of each party involved? As the Owner, if they have an in-house Commissioning Manager, they may need to review and approve technical documents submitted by the Commissioning Agent, including Specifications, Commissioning Plans, Commissioning Forms, and the final report for the commissioning phase. The Owner will oversee some commissioning activities (Cx Activities) but will not be involved throughout the entire process. If the Owner does not have dedicated personnel or departments, they will rely entirely on the design team or contractors to complete the relevant work.

For retrofit projects in existing buildings, such as partial renovations of large structures (e.g., renovating only one floor), the building owner must collaborate with the General Contractor (GC) to provide Base Building Support. This includes sharing building system information, As-Built Drawings, operation and maintenance documents (O&M Manuals), and details about the existing operations team to offer technical support to the commissioning team.

The primary responsibility of the GC is to coordinate with subcontractors (Sub Trades). The Commissioning Agent does not perform hands-on tasks directly but guides the GC’s testing contractors (Test Contractors), equipment suppliers (Vendors), or control system contractors (Control Contractors) to complete testing activities and commissioning deliverables.

The commissioning work is indeed related to this. For instance, when commissioning a piece of equipment, it is necessary to refer to the technical parameters of the equipment as indicated in the shop drawings. The O&M manuals are also the final documents that the commissioning agent needs to collect. These two types of documents also require review and approval by the consultant.

The consultant may participate in some testing, commissioning, or even training activities, but this is not mandatory and entirely depends on the terms of the service agreement signed between the consultant and the client. The contract must clearly specify the number of commissioning meetings the consultant is required to attend; otherwise, they may refuse to participate if it exceeds the contract scope.

Additionally, the consultant is also responsible for preparing the snag list, conducting on-site inspections, and reviewing relevant documents. The specific responsibilities of the consultant during the construction phase were explained in detail in the previous lesson and will not be reiterated here. The commissioning agent is actually responsible for the majority of the work.

He needs to be involved in all commissioning-related work. He is required to chair meetings, prepare meeting minutes, develop commissioning plans, and organize/supervise/witness all testing and commissioning activities. Additionally, he must review and approve test reports submitted by subcontractors (such as control contractors or testing contractors).

He is responsible for compiling commissioning reports and reviewing/approving the Operation & Maintenance Manuals. Another critical document is the Completion Dossier, also known as the Handover Dossier. Throughout the commissioning process, he must coordinate with the client, general contractor, consultants, and subcontractors. Ultimately, he will submit the complete Final Handover Dossier.

The process primarily involves mechanical contractors, electrical contractors, and control contractors, who are responsible for conducting specific tests. These tests must be performed under the guidance of the commissioning agent, and upon completion, forms must be filled out to submit the test results or reports to the consultant and commissioning agent for review.

The commissioning agent supervises on-site, but for large-scale projects, it is impractical to inspect every system and equipment commissioning step individually. Therefore, they typically conduct random sampling—checking two or three out of 100 air conditioning units—while the remaining units are commissioned by the contractors themselves. The commissioning agent may instead focus on inspecting central plant equipment such as boilers and cooling towers.

Contractors must follow the agreed-upon testing procedures and standards, documenting results during the process. As subcontractors, they must sign off on the results, take responsibility for them, and then compile and submit the results to the commissioning agent and consultant for review.

If the results meet requirements, the project proceeds to the next phase. If issues arise—for instance, failing to meet the design specifications for indoor temperature control—retesting is required. Should the problem persist after retesting (e.g., inadequate cooling capacity preventing the system from meeting demand), the issue falls outside the scope of the contractors and commissioning agent, requiring resolution by the design team.

Rather, it is the design consultant’s design that has issues. In such cases, the problem must be raised and a solution negotiated with the client and the consultant. If no resolution is possible, confirmation must be signed by the relevant parties. This is not the responsibility of the construction contract or the commissioning agent, but rather the design team’s obligation.

Subcontractors must provide manpower, equipment, and tools, including ladders, radios, laptops, and other necessary items. For example, during fire alarm testing, subcontractors or suppliers must provide smoke generators, sound level meters, illuminance meters, and other required equipment. In the final training phase, training can be conducted by subcontractors, the in-house team, or hired suppliers.

For equipment system suppliers or manufacturers, their responsibility is to provide startup support services. During the initial startup of air handling units or generators, they must ensure the equipment is fully operational before leaving the site. The specific duration of on-site support depends on contract terms. When signing contracts with subcontractors or suppliers, startup testing requirements, BIS system arrangements, and provisions for the final training phase must be included.

During the design phase, we need to review multiple design documents, including the design package from the Basic Design Consultant. Typically, we review the basic design and the 66% design package, which is the DD (Design Development) stage package, and participate in design meetings.

Upon entering the CD (Construction Documentation) stage, we not only review the technical documents from the design consultant but also need to prepare relevant documents ourselves. These documents include the Commissioning Plan, Commissioning Specifications, as well as sample inspection and testing procedures. These procedures are usually presented in tabular or sequential formats, covering individual system or equipment tests, as well as integrated system tests. I will showcase these sample documents later.

During the construction phase, we also need to review Construction Drawings.

Of course, our current discussion focuses on reviewing shop drawings from the perspective of the commissioning agent. We won’t devote excessive effort because the review prioritizes the commissioning viewpoint rather than conducting a comprehensive examination like consultants. Therefore, as commissioning agents, the time spent reviewing shop drawings is relatively limited, given that consultants bear primary responsibility.

During the construction phase, if previously submitted commissioning deliverables—including specifications, plans, or procedures—require modifications, these changes must strictly adhere to the IFC design package from the construction process. When design consultants update drawings, it is necessary to identify which sections require adjustments. For example, if the original design package’s commissioning deliverables included five air handling units but one was removed or IIS equipment was added during the IFC stage, these changes must be reflected in the commissioning plan and test procedures. This is a routine technical update task.

Additionally, commissioning agents must participate in construction meetings and respond to commissioning-related RFIs. Typically, commissioning agents have lighter workloads during the tender phase.
